name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,370

clue.text: Trouble following idiot’s attack (6)

indicators.note: What follows something comes along behind it, so the letters named in front of the word are written second.

blocks.note: an ass is a fool, the donkey used of people
to ail somebody is to trouble them — what ails you?

explanation.surface: Trouble arriving in the wake of a fool's outburst.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following' is the instruction that fixes the order: in an across entry, what follows is written second. Ail is the old verb for trouble, still alive in 'what ails you'.
explanation.definitionFit: To assail someone is to attack them, whether with fists or with questions, so the two verbs swap straight over.

clue.text: American clubs repeatedly exploited defendant (7)

indicators.note: Something done repeatedly happens more than once, so the letter just named is written out twice.

blocks.note: A is the standard short form of American
C is clubs among the card suits, set down twice as the instruction beside it asks
to exploit a thing is to use it

explanation.surface: An American whose clubs were played again and again now stands in the dock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exploited' is wanted in its plain sense of put to use, with none of the unfairness the surface loads into it. C is the clubs suit at bridge.
explanation.definitionFit: The accused is the person answering a criminal charge in court, which is exactly who the defendant is.

clue.text: Southern seabird’s back (5)

blocks.note: S is southern, the letter on the compass
a tern is a slim white seabird with a forked tail

explanation.surface: A seabird from the south, seen from behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' is a noun here, the rear end of a boat, and not the instruction to reverse anything that it looks like. The tern is the crossword's standing seabird.
explanation.definitionFit: The stern is the rear end of a ship, so 'back' is the plain noun for the part it names.

clue.text: Fancy telling niece what CIA is after! (12)

indicators.note: To fancy something up is to do it over in another style, and letters done over come out in a new arrangement.

blocks.note: seven letters of fodder, the word taken for its spelling alone
five more, making the twelve the grid wants

explanation.surface: Mock astonishment that anyone would tell a niece what the CIA is chasing.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is four words long and not one of them is a synonym: it describes the answer by what an agency wants rather than naming it. 'Fancy' opens the clue as mock surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: Intelligence is the trade word for gathered secret information, and collecting it is precisely what an agency like the CIA exists to do.

clue.text: Get what shipwrecked sea dog longs for? (4)

definitions.text: what shipwrecked sea dog longs for

blocks.note: the plain verb for obtaining something you were after — a job, a contract, a part

blocks.clueFragment: what shipwrecked sea dog longs for
blocks.note: a sailor cast away on the water wants one thing in sight, and it is dry ground

explanation.surface: A marooned old sailor staring at the horizon and wishing for one thing.
explanation.walkthrough: Land a job, land a contract — the verb means to secure, and that is the half that hides. The second half is a picture rather than a dictionary phrase, which is what the question mark owns up to.
explanation.definitionFit: To land something is to get it, and dry land is what a castaway sailor is longing to reach — the same four letters from both directions.

clue.text: A bishop by himself eating this? (7)

definitions.text: A bishop by himself eating this?

blocks.note: the word itself, taken straight
B is the bishop on a chessboard
a man by himself is alone

explanation.surface: A bishop taking his supper on his own.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This' points at the word you are about to write in, so there is no separate definition to hunt down. Read straight, the whole sentence is a picture of the answer on a plate.
explanation.definitionFit: Abalone is an edible sea snail served as a delicacy, so the sentence read straight is a bishop dining alone on the answer.

clue.text: Fear old man is catching on (5)

indicators.note: To catch a thing is to take hold of it and keep it, so the word doing the catching closes around the letters named next.

blocks.note: the old man is the British way of saying one's father
RE is the abbreviation at the head of a memo, meaning on or concerning

explanation.surface: An old man who is quick to pick things up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catching' in the surface is the sense a cold is catching, and in the wordplay the sense of taking hold. RE for 'on' is the memo heading, the one that means concerning.
explanation.definitionFit: Dread is fear of something still to come — the noun for the cold weight of it — so 'Fear' is the plain synonym.

clue.text: Farm animal eating hot dog (4)

indicators.note: Whatever is eaten ends up inside the eater, so the letters named next are set within the ones just found.

blocks.note: the cow is the farm animal, and it opens up to hold what follows
H is hot, the letter on a British tap

explanation.surface: A cow working its way through a hot dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot dog' is the trap: read the two words together as the food and the clue is left with no definition at all. The chow chow is a thick-coated Chinese breed with a blue-black tongue.
explanation.definitionFit: A chow is a breed of dog — the stocky chow chow — so 'dog' names the answer by its kind.

clue.text: Alienation of curious people in Spielberg film (12)

indicators.note: What is in a thing sits inside it, so the letters just named are set between the letters of the word that follows.

blocks.note: E.T. is Spielberg's 1982 film, its title the initials the boy's alien friend goes by
curious in the sense of odd rather than inquisitive
men are people, the plural taken loosely

explanation.surface: Odd people turning up in a Steven Spielberg picture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Curious' has two senses and the wanted one is odd, not inquisitive. The two-letter film title splits to take in nine letters, so the join is nowhere near the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Estrangement is the state of two people who have become alienated from one another, so 'Alienation' is the plain noun for it.

clue.text: Spotted African runner — adulterer they say (7)

indicators.note: What people say is the sound of a word and not its spelling, so the answer is what the word named sounds like rather than how it is written.

blocks.note: an adulterer cheats on a partner, so he is a cheater; said aloud, that is the big cat

explanation.surface: A spotted African sprinter named in the same breath as an unfaithful husband.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash does the work of an equals sign: the two halves match in sound, not in sense. Cheetahs are the fastest animal on land, which is what makes 'runner' fair.
explanation.definitionFit: The cheetah is a spotted big cat of Africa and the fastest sprinter alive, so all three words of the definition land on it.

clue.text: Brash American hiding embarrassment (5)

indicators.note: Something hiding is concealed inside what surrounds it, so the answer is sitting unbroken in the words as they are written.

blocks.note: the run takes the last two letters of the first word and the first three of the second

explanation.surface: A loud-mouthed American keeping his blushes to himself.
explanation.walkthrough: The run straddles the gap between two words, which is where hidden answers are hardest to see. 'Brash American' is in the clue for no reason but the letters it carries.
explanation.definitionFit: Shame is the hot discomfort of having been humiliated, which is what embarrassment names.

clue.text: Star female put down oil producer (9)

blocks.note: the sun is a star, the nearest one
F is the short form of female, the letter on a form
to put something down is to lower it

explanation.surface: A famous woman running down somebody in the oil business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put down' is the verb lower rather than the insult it sounds like, and the star wanted is the one in the sky. Sunflower oil is pressed from the seeds of the head.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunflower seeds are pressed for cooking oil, so the plant is defined by what it yields rather than by any synonym.

clue.text: Elderly husband avoiding embrace (3)

indicators.note: To avoid a thing is to keep out of it, so the letter just named never appears in the word that follows.

blocks.note: an embrace is a hold, arriving here without the letter named in front of it
H is the standard short form of husband, and it is the letter kept out

explanation.surface: An old man steering clear of a hug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elderly husband' reads as one phrase, but the break falls after the first word. H beside 'husband' is the letter a form asks for.
explanation.definitionFit: Old and elderly both say advanced in years; elderly is only the politer of the two.

clue.text: Briefly express view after doctor’s visit (4,2)

indicators.note: Say a thing briefly and you cut it short, so the word named arrives without its last letter.
What comes after something is written behind it, so these letters follow the ones named next.

blocks.note: DR is the two letters on a surgery nameplate
to express a view is to opine, stopped one letter short as the instruction asks

explanation.surface: Giving a quick verdict once the doctor has been round.
explanation.walkthrough: A drop-in is an unannounced call, so the answer is a noun where the two words read as a verb. 'Briefly' shortens the opinion, not the doctor — DR is already as short as it gets.
explanation.definitionFit: A drop-in is a short unannounced call on somebody, which is what 'visit' names as a noun.

clue.text: Choose one parent as model (7)

blocks.note: to choose between things is to opt for one
one is the Roman numeral I
mum is the British word for mother, and a mother is a parent

explanation.surface: Picking one of your parents as the person to copy.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'one parent' as a single idea where the wordplay wants two separate pieces. 'As' does nothing but join the halves together.
explanation.definitionFit: An optimum is the best available version of a thing, and a model in the sense of an ideal to copy is that best case held up as a standard.

clue.text: Heartlessly examine very small creature (6)

indicators.note: Something heartless has had its middle taken out, so the letter standing at the centre of the word named goes missing.

blocks.note: to examine a thing is to inspect it, and the instruction in front strips out the letter at its centre

explanation.surface: Looking somebody over without an ounce of pity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heartlessly' reads as cruelly on the surface and as an instruction underneath. The heart of a seven-letter word is its single middle letter, so exactly one goes.
explanation.definitionFit: An insect is a six-legged creature small enough to sit on a fingernail, so the definition names it by size and kind.

clue.text: Picture intact, I suspect (7)

indicators.note: To call a thing suspect is to say it is not what it appears to be, and letters that are not what they appear need putting back in another order.

blocks.note: six letters of fodder, the word taken for its spelling alone
the speaker of the clue, worth one letter

explanation.surface: Doubting aloud that something has come through undamaged.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma after 'intact' is there for the surface alone; the letters run straight across it. The ship the film is named for ended up the opposite of intact.
explanation.definitionFit: A picture is a motion picture, and Titanic is one — James Cameron's film of 1997 — so the definition names it by its kind.

clue.text: Fate of item for sale at Sotheby’s (3)

blocks.note: the portion that falls to a person in life, whatever they are dealt
an auction house numbers everything it puts up, and each numbered item is one of these

explanation.surface: The destiny hanging over something about to go under the hammer.
explanation.walkthrough: Sotheby's is the London auction house, and every item it offers is catalogued as a numbered lot. 'Fate' is the older sense, the lot you are cast in life.
explanation.definitionFit: Your lot is the fate dealt to you, and a lot is also the numbered item an auctioneer puts up for bidding.

clue.text: Clear line head of UK police supports (5)

indicators.note: The head of a word is its front end, so only the first letter of the one named is wanted.
Whatever supports a thing stands underneath it, and in a down entry underneath means later in the answer.

blocks.note: L is the short form of line
the front letter of the two, as the instruction beside it asks
the CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, the plain-clothes detective branch of a British police force

explanation.surface: A UK police chief getting behind a particular line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supports' reads as backing a policy and does the crossword job of putting the police at the foot of the column. It only works that way because this entry runs down.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucid means clear and easy to follow — a lucid explanation — and also clear-headed, as in a lucid interval.

clue.text: Emir’s text disturbed fanatic (9)

indicators.note: Something disturbed has been knocked out of the arrangement it was in, so these letters will not stay in the order they were handed over.

blocks.note: five letters of fodder, the apostrophe counting for nothing
four more, making the nine the grid wants

explanation.surface: A zealot throwing an emir's message into confusion.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s belongs to the fodder rather than to the grammar, which is how the count reaches nine. 'Disturbed' reads as an adjective describing the fanatic.
explanation.definitionFit: An extremist holds views at the far end of the spectrum and acts on them, which is what 'fanatic' names as a noun.

clue.text: Roman attire, article acquired from the south (4)

indicators.note: A down entry is read from the top downwards, so anything coming up from the south arrives the other way about.

blocks.note: acquired is GOT, written from its far end as the instruction asks
A is the indefinite article, a single letter the turn leaves as it was

explanation.surface: A piece of Roman dress picked up somewhere down south.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From the south' can only mean upwards because this entry runs down the grid; in an across clue it would say nothing at all. 'Acquired' is wanted in its past tense.
explanation.definitionFit: The toga is the draped woollen garment a Roman citizen wore in public, so 'Roman attire' names it by its people and its kind.

clue.text: Popular place to rent in bay (5)

blocks.note: what is popular this season is in
a property put on the market for rent is a let

explanation.surface: A fashionable rental property overlooking the water.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue uses 'in' twice over: the first is the word for fashionable, the second only a joint between the halves. A let is what a landlord calls the property itself.
explanation.definitionFit: An inlet is a narrow recess of sea running into the land, which is what a bay is.

clue.text: Funny business with the Speaker’s assistant? (5)

blocks.note: CO is the short form of company on a firm's letterhead
a mic is the microphone that helps anyone speaking be heard, short for the full word

explanation.surface: Some funny dealings involving the aide who works for the Speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital S sells the Speaker of the Commons and his staff; the assistant wanted is the microphone a speaker talks into. The question mark covers that leap.
explanation.definitionFit: Comic is the adjective for anything meant to raise a laugh, so it swaps straight in for 'Funny'.

clue.text: Men upset with girl, mischievous little thing (7)

indicators.note: To upset something is to tip it over and spill what was in it, so its letters come out in no order at all.

blocks.note: three letters of fodder, the word taken for its spelling alone
four more, making the seven the grid wants

explanation.surface: Men falling out with a girl over some small troublemaker.
explanation.walkthrough: Gremlins were the imps RAF crews blamed for the faults that appeared in their aircraft. 'Upset' reads as annoyed in the surface and as a spill underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: A gremlin is a small invisible sprite invented to explain machinery going wrong, so it is mischief in a little body.

clue.text: Furious about knight’s curse (4)

indicators.note: To turn about is to come round and face the other way, so the letters it is applied to are written out backwards.

blocks.note: furious is MAD, set down from its far end as the instruction beside it asks
N is the knight in chess notation, K having gone to the king

explanation.surface: An angry outburst aimed at a knight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' turns the first word only; the knight is added afterwards rather than caught up in the turn. It reads on the surface as being angry concerning somebody.
explanation.definitionFit: To damn someone is to curse them, to call down ruin on them, so the two verbs swap straight over.

clue.text: Some resist a tickle still (6)

indicators.note: Some of a thing is a part taken out of it, so the answer is a run of letters sitting in the words as they are written.

blocks.note: the run begins in the last two letters of the first word and ends in the first three of the last

explanation.surface: People who can still hold out against being tickled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' is the adjective meaning motionless, not the adverb the surface uses it as. The run spans three words, which is what buries it so well.
explanation.definitionFit: Static means not moving and not changing — a static population stays exactly where it is — which is what 'still' says.
